title: Organic Chemistry
tagline: Why carbon builds its own chemistry: tetravalency, catenation, the homologous series and the two reactions that rule them all.

overview.intro: Organic chemistry is the chemistry of carbon compounds, and the syllabus wants you to understand why carbon deserves its own subject. Three properties — tetravalency, catenation and the stability of its bonds — let carbon chain, branch and ring itself into millions of compounds, and the same repeating patterns make that complexity manageable. This chapter builds from the atom to the homologous series, nomenclature and isomerism, then works through alkanes, alkenes and alkynes so that substitution and addition become predictable rather than memorised.

facts.label: Tetravalency
facts.value: Carbon forms four bonds, allowing a huge variety of arrangements around one atom.

facts.label: Catenation
facts.value: Carbon atoms join to each other to form long chains, branches and rings.

facts.label: Homologous series
facts.value: Family of compounds differing by CH2, with a common general formula and similar properties.

facts.label: Two reaction types
facts.value: Substitution in saturated compounds, addition across the double or triple bond.

learningOutcomes: Explain the unique position of carbon in the periodic table using tetravalency and catenation.
Define a homologous series and state the four features that characterise one.
Name and write formulae for members of the alkane, alkene and alkyne series up to four carbons.
Distinguish structural isomerism and give the isomers of a named alkane.
Write equations for the substitution of methane and the addition reactions of ethene, explaining which bonds break.

blocks.text: Carbon sits in group 14 with four valence electrons, which means it must share rather than lose or gain to reach a stable octet, and it can form four such shared pairs. That tetravalency alone is unusual but not unique; what makes carbon exceptional is the second property, catenation — the ability of an atom to bond to others of its own kind to give chains of almost any length. Carbon does this better than any other element because the C–C bond is strong and not easily attacked by the reagents that break the chains of silicon and heavier congeners. Put the two together and the possibilities multiply: straight chains, branched chains, rings, and every combination of them, with hydrogen, halogen, oxygen and nitrogen attached at chosen points. From this single fact follows the size of organic chemistry: millions of compounds built from one element’s two habits.

items: Tetravalency: carbon forms four bonds and never exceeds an octet in normal compounds.
Catenation: C–C bonds are strong and stable, allowing long chains, branches and rings.
Carbon bonds to itself and to H, O, N, halogens and other carbons, giving enormous structural variety.
Multiple bonding: carbon forms single, double and triple bonds, which opens the door to unsaturated chemistry.

items.note: Butane holds four carbons in a row, each saturated with hydrogen to the formula C4H10.
Isobutane uses the same atoms but branches them, giving different properties from the same formula.

items.meaning: Valence of four, giving carbon four bonds in its compounds.
Self-linking of atoms, here carbon atoms forming chains and rings.
Containing only single carbon-carbon bonds, so no more atoms can be added.
Containing a double or triple carbon-carbon bond that can open to add atoms.

blocks.text: Organic chemistry becomes manageable because compounds fall into families called homologous series. Every member differs from the next by a CH2 group, shares the same general formula, shows a gradual trend in physical properties, and undergoes the same type of chemical reaction because it contains the same functional group. The alkane series follows CnH2n+2, the alkenes CnH2n with one double bond, and the alkynes CnH2n-2 with a triple bond. Naming follows a simple rule: count the longest chain, take the root from the number of carbons — meth, eth, prop, but — and add the ending -ane, -ene or -yne. Physical properties change predictably along the series: as the chain grows, the molecules get heavier and the intermolecular forces strengthen, so boiling points rise and the lower members are gases while the higher ones are liquids and eventually solids.

items: Members differ by CH2 and their molecular masses differ by 14 units.
General formulae: alkanes CnH2n+2, alkenes CnH2n, alkynes Cn2n-2.
Boiling points rise down a series as molecular size and van der Waals forces increase.
Chemical properties are similar within a series because the same functional group is present.

blocks.caption: The first four members of each series

items.note: Four carbons in a saturated chain is butane, C4H10; remove two hydrogens to make a double bond and it becomes butene, C4H8.
Pentene has five carbons and one double bond, so its formula is C5H10 from the alkene general formula.

blocks.text: Two compounds can share an identical molecular formula and still be different substances, and the reason is that the atoms are connected differently. These are structural isomers, and the standard example is butane: a straight chain of four carbons gives one arrangement, while the same four carbons arranged with a three-carbon chain and a one-carbon branch gives another, named 2-methylpropane. Both are C4H10, both burn to give carbon dioxide and water, but their boiling points differ because molecular shape affects how the molecules pack together. Isomerism is what makes counting formulae misleading — a molecular formula identifies composition, not structure — and it is why IUPAC names exist: a name must pick out exactly one arrangement.

items: Structural isomers have the same molecular formula but different atom-to-atom connections.
Chain isomerism changes the carbon skeleton, as in butane against 2-methylpropane.
Position isomerism moves a functional group or multiple bond along the chain, as in but-1-ene against but-2-ene.
Different structures give different physical properties, most visibly in boiling point.

items.note: Both C4H10; the branched isomer boils lower because its compact shape reduces contact between molecules.
Both C4H8; the double bond sits on carbon 1 in one and carbon 2 in the other.

items.meaning: Compounds with the same molecular formula but different structural formulae.
Isomerism arising from a different arrangement of the carbon skeleton.
Isomerism arising from a functional group or multiple bond in a different position.

blocks.text: Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons containing only single bonds, and their chemistry reflects that stability. They burn in excess air to give carbon dioxide and water with a hot blue flame, which is why methane, propane and butane are fuels. In the dark, an alkane reacts with chlorine by substitution: one hydrogen at a time is replaced by chlorine and hydrogen chloride is released, and the reaction needs ultraviolet light to start because it is a free-radical chain process. Each substitution step gives the next member of a chloride series, so careful control of the chlorine-to-alkane ratio decides which product dominates. Alkanes resist attack by acids, alkalis and oxidising agents at room temperature — the same inertness that makes them useful as solvents and as the unreactive component of petroleum.

items: Complete combustion gives carbon dioxide and water; incomplete combustion gives carbon monoxide or soot.
Substitution in ultraviolet light: CH4 + Cl2 → CH3Cl + HCl, continuing through further substitutions.
Alkanes are unreactive at room temperature because C–C and C–H bonds are strong and non-polar.
The first four members are gases, then liquids with rising boiling point up the series.

items.note: CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O, releasing the heat that makes natural gas a fuel.
Ultraviolet light breaks chlorine into radicals that strip a hydrogen and attach chlorine instead.

learn.title: Alkenes, alkynes and the addition reaction

blocks.text: Remove two hydrogens from adjacent carbons and the single bond becomes a double bond: the compound is unsaturated and its chemistry changes completely. The double bond consists of a strong sigma bond and a weaker pi bond, and it is the pi bond that opens up during reactions, allowing atoms to add across it without anything being displaced. That is addition: hydrogen adds to give the alkane, halogens add across the bond and lose their colour, and hydrogen halides add according to Markovnikov’s pattern with the hydrogen joining the carbon that already holds more hydrogens. Alkynes carry a triple bond and behave similarly, taking up two molecules of reagent in two steps. Because the halogen addition reaction destroys the brown or purple colour of bromine and iodine solution, it doubles as the test for unsaturation — the practical sign that a double or triple bond is present.

items: Addition of hydrogen (hydrogenation) converts an alkene into the corresponding alkane with a nickel catalyst.
Addition of bromine decolourises the reagent, which is the standard test for unsaturation.
Addition of hydrogen halide follows Markovnikov’s rule: hydrogen attaches to the carbon with more hydrogens.
Alkynes add two molecules of reagent because they hold a triple bond.

items.note: The reddish-brown bromine colour disappears as 1,2-dibromoethane forms, proving a double bond.
CH2=CH2 + H2 → CH3CH3 over heated nickel, converting the unsaturated gas into ethane.

items.meaning: Reaction in which atoms add across a multiple bond, opening it without anything being displaced.
Addition of hydrogen to an unsaturated compound, usually with a metal catalyst.
Decolourisation of bromine water indicating a carbon-carbon multiple bond.
In hydrogen halide addition, hydrogen joins the carbon already bearing the greater number of hydrogens.

keyPoints: Carbon is tetravalent and shows strong catenation, which together allow chains, branches and rings.
A homologous series differs by CH2, shares a general formula, and shows similar chemical properties.
General formulae: alkanes CnH2n+2, alkenes Cn2n, alkynes Cn2n-2.
Boiling points rise down a homologous series as molecular size and intermolecular forces increase.
Structural isomers share a molecular formula but differ in the connections of their atoms.
Alkanes burn to carbon dioxide and water and undergo substitution with chlorine in ultraviolet light.
Alkenes and alkynes are unsaturated and undergo addition across the multiple bond.
Bromine decolourisation is the standard test for unsaturation.
Hydrogenation converts an alkene to an alkane over a nickel catalyst.
Markovnikov’s rule predicts where hydrogen adds when a hydrogen halide joins an unsymmetrical alkene.
examFocus: Explain carbon’s position with both properties — tetravalency and catenation — because half an answer earns half a mark.
Structural formulae must show every bond between carbons; condensed formulae are not enough when isomerism is asked.
State the conditions for substitution (ultraviolet light) separately from those for addition (usually a catalyst or nothing).
The unsaturation test is a two-part answer: add bromine water, observe the colour disappear.

questions.prompt: The general formula of the alkane series is:
questions.explanation: Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons, so with n carbons they carry 2n + 2 hydrogens.

questions.prompt: Decolourisation of bromine water by a hydrocarbon shows that it is:
questions.explanation: Bromine adds across a carbon-carbon multiple bond, so loss of colour proves unsaturation.
Both have the formula C4H10 but differ in the arrangement of their carbon chains.

questions.prompt: The reaction of methane with chlorine in ultraviolet light is classified as:
questions.explanation: A hydrogen atom is replaced by chlorine while hydrogen chloride is displaced, which is substitution.

questions.prompt: The tendency of carbon atoms to bond to one another in long chains is called __________.
questions.explanation: Catenation together with tetravalency explains why carbon forms such a vast range of compounds.

questions.prompt: A family of compounds differing by a CH2 group and sharing a general formula is called a homologous __________.
questions.explanation: Members of one series differ by CH2 and therefore by 14 units of molecular mass.

questions.prompt: State two properties of carbon that make it the basis of a separate branch of chemistry.
questions.answer: Tetravalency, which lets each carbon form four bonds, and catenation, which lets carbon atoms link to one another to form long chains, branches and rings. Together they allow an enormous variety of stable structures to be built from one element.
questions.explanation: Four bonds provide the connections and self-linking provides the framework on which they arrange.

questions.prompt: Give the molecular formulae of butane and butene and explain the difference.
questions.answer: Butane is C4H10 and butene is C4H8. Each carbon holds four bonds, so the saturated four-carbon chain takes ten hydrogens, while one double bond in butene removes two hydrogens to keep every carbon at four bonds.
questions.explanation: Each multiple bond costs two hydrogen atoms relative to the saturated formula.

questions.prompt: What is observed when a colourless alkene is shaken with bromine water?
questions.answer: The reddish-brown colour of the bromine water disappears because bromine adds across the double bond to give a colourless dibromo compound.
questions.explanation: The test is positive for unsaturation and negative for a saturated hydrocarbon.

questions.prompt: Describe the reaction of methane with chlorine in ultraviolet light, name the product and explain why it is not an addition reaction.
questions.answer: In ultraviolet light chlorine molecules split into chlorine radicals. A radical abstracts a hydrogen atom from methane, forming a methyl radical and hydrogen chloride; the methyl radical then attacks another chlorine molecule to give chloromethane and regenerates a radical, so the reaction is a chain process. Further substitution can replace additional hydrogens to give dichloromethane, chloroform and carbon tetrachloride if chlorine is in excess. It is substitution rather than addition because methane is saturated: it has no multiple bond to open, so an atom must be displaced for another to take its place, and hydrogen chloride leaves as a separate product.
questions.explanation: Saturated molecules cannot add, so replacement of hydrogen by chlorine is the only feasible route, and the displaced hydrogen forms a second product.

questions.prompt: Explain why boiling points rise through a homologous series, and illustrate your answer with methane and butane.
questions.answer: Boiling a liquid means overcoming the attractive forces between its molecules, not breaking the covalent bonds inside them. In a homologous series each member has a longer carbon chain and a greater molecular mass, so there is more surface area over which the weak van der Waals forces can act and more electrons to be polarised at any instant. The attraction between molecules therefore grows steadily with chain length. Methane, the smallest member, is a gas at room temperature because its tiny molecules attract each other only weakly, while butane, four carbons long, has much stronger intermolecular attraction and condenses to a liquid at temperatures where methane remains a gas.
questions.explanation: Intermolecular forces scale with molecular size, and those are the forces boiling must overcome.

questions.prompt: A colourless hydrocarbon decolourises bromine water, and on hydrogenation over heated nickel it absorbs hydrogen to give a saturated product of formula C4H10. Identify the original compound’s series and molecular formula, and explain how the two observations together prove your answer.
questions.answer: The decolourisation of bromine water proves the compound is unsaturated, so it contains a carbon-carbon double or triple bond. Hydrogenation absorbing hydrogen to reach C4H10 shows the starting material was two hydrogens short of the saturated formula, which places it in the alkene series with the formula C4H8. Alkynes would have been four hydrogens short and would have taken up two molecules of hydrogen to reach an alkane of the same carbon count; since the saturated product is C4H10, the reactant is butene. Together, one test shows the presence of a multiple bond and the other counts how many there were.
questions.explanation: Unsaturation plus the amount of hydrogen absorbed distinguishes an alkene from an alkyne and fixes the molecular formula.
